what_its_for: Naltrexone is used to help people stop drinking alcohol or to help people who have stopped using opioid drugs (like heroin or prescription pain pills) stay off them. It works by blocking the 'feel-good' effects that alcohol and opioids cause in your brain, making it easier to resist the urge to use them. It is not a cure, but it is a helpful tool when used together with counseling and support programs.
how_to_take: Naltrexone comes as a tablet (pill) you swallow once a day, or as an injection (shot) given by your doctor once a month. Take the tablet at the same time each day, with or without food. If the pill upsets your stomach, try taking it with food or a small snack. Never crush, chew, or break the tablet. The monthly injection (Vivitrol) is given in your doctor's office — you should NOT try to give this shot to yourself at home. Before starting naltrexone, make sure you have NOT used any opioid drugs for at least 7 to 10 days. Taking naltrexone while opioids are still in your body can cause sudden, severe withdrawal symptoms.
dosing: For the tablet (ReVia): The usual adult dose is 50 mg once daily. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose and slowly increase it. For the monthly injection (Vivitrol): The usual dose is 380 mg given as a shot into your buttocks muscle once every 4 weeks by your healthcare provider. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose of the tablet, take it as soon as you remember — UNLESS it is almost time for your next dose. If your next dose is coming up soon, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you miss your monthly injection appointment, call your doctor right away to reschedule as soon as possible.
storage: Store naltrexone tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep them away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do NOT store them in the bathroom. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. The monthly injection (Vivitrol) is stored and handled by your doctor's office — you do not need to worry about storing it at home.
what_to_avoid: Do NOT use any opioid drugs (heroin, morphine, oxycodone, hydrocodone, codeine, fentanyl, methadone, tramadol, etc.) while taking naltrexone. Naltrexone will block the effects of opioids, and if you use large amounts of opioids trying to 'feel' them, you could overdose and die. Avoid alcohol if you are being treated for opioid dependence. Do not take any over-the-counter products that contain opioids, such as certain cough medicines or diarrhea medications (like loperamide in high doses). Tell all of your doctors and pharmacists that you are taking naltrexone before getting any new medicines or procedures.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice: yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes (jaundice), dark urine, severe stomach pain or vomiting, unusual tiredness, or loss of appetite — these could be signs of liver problems. Also seek help immediately if you feel suddenly sick, have severe withdrawal symptoms (shaking, sweating, stomach cramps, vomiting, diarrhea), feel very depressed or have thoughts of hurting yourself, have an allergic reaction (trouble breathing, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, rash, or hives), or notice pain, swelling, redness, or a lump at your injection site that does not go away.
when_it_works: Naltrexone starts blocking opioid effects within 1 to 2 hours of taking a dose. However, for alcohol cravings, it may take a few weeks of regular use before you notice the full benefit. The monthly injection maintains a steady level of medicine in your body for the full 4 weeks. Remember, naltrexone works best when combined with a counseling program, support groups, and other recovery tools. Many people begin to see improvements in their cravings and ability to stay sober within the first few weeks of treatment.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before using naltrexone if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. It is not fully known how naltrexone affects an unborn baby or breast milk. Liver or kidney problems: Naltrexone is processed by your liver and kidneys. Tell your doctor if you have any liver or kidney disease, because your dose may need to be adjusted or naltrexone may not be right for you. Children and teenagers: Naltrexone is generally approved for adults. Its safety and effectiveness in children have not been fully studied. Older adults: Older adults may be more sensitive to the effects of naltrexone and should be monitored closely by their doctor.
